"But it works!" is the most common remark from students when they receive suggestions from the teachers. While a problem can be solved with code written in different ways that produce the same results, some solutions are certainly more efficient or readable than others. In programming, there are industry standards for code quality, efficiency, and readability. So simply getting the code to work may not be enough. But reaching a professional level takes time and plenty of coding experience. What matters most is that you're open to learning and to your teachers' advice.

We can sometimes overthink and add redundant blocks to our code. Making our code concise (short and clear) is one way to keep it tidy and easy to debug.

Below is a sample code. Simplify it as much as you can while ensuring it still produces the same results.

Look for repetitions and see if they can be grouped together.

Why do we care so much about code efficiency, anyway? Well, if you're working on a real project, whether it's your own game for fun or a confidential, world-changing application for your startup, it’s likely to grow into a large and complex program.

Hence, writing efficient code from the start isn’t just about elegance. It’s about scalability, maintainability, and keeping bugs at bay. As your program grows, every redundant line or inefficient structure can snowball into sluggish performance and difficult debugging. Efficient code not only makes your project faster, it also makes collaboration smoother, especially when others need to read, understand, or build upon your work.

Let's try out another example code. Simplify it as much as you can while ensuring it still produces the same results.


Look for redundant (unnecessary) blocks.

When creating application, user experience is very important. We call this user-friendliness. A poor program design can make a good idea fail. Hence, always consider how users will feel when they use your application for the first time.

Mr. Slowy created a simple remote-control car. The player just has to press one button to start it, then use two others to control the steering. He wrote this code, and while it seems perfectly logical, everyone says it's bad programming. Can you test it out and figure out how it can be improved?


A frozen app doesn’t always mean broken logic. Sometimes it’s just slow because time adds up. Peek inside the code to see what’s causing delays.
